summary: This revision extends a prior toy-domain study isolating two conflated sources of semantic entropy's (SE) advantage over cheaper uncertainty proxies (sampling at all vs. clustering by meaning) with two new experiments that directly address the round-1 review's main weaknesses: a synthetic paraphrase-noise sweep that reintroduces surface-form ambiguity to show SE genuinely beats self-consistency once clustering rules diverge (AUROC gap grows from -0.001 at noise_p=0 to +0.022 at noise_p=0.9, p<0.001), and a 3-seed replication showing the SE≈SC≈NLL≫TE pattern is not an artifact of one training run. I reran all three provided scripts (experiment.py, paraphrase_experiment.py, seed_experiment.py) end-to-end on CPU and every reported number reproduced exactly, including AUROCs, p-values, and wall-clock times.
strengths:
- Full reproducibility verified independently: I ran `python paraphrase_experiment.py` and got AUROC_SE=0.9861 (constant) vs AUROC_SC=0.9876/0.9849/0.9726/0.9637 at noise_p=0/0.3/0.6/0.9 with p=0.54/0.63/0.03/<0.001 — matching Table in §3 exactly; I ran `python seed_experiment.py` and got seed0/1/2 SE/SC/NLL/TE values matching the paper's replication table to 3+ decimal places; wall-clock times (89s and 296s) matched the claimed ~90s and ~5min
- The paraphrase-noise experiment is a genuine methodological addition, not just a rerun: it directly tests the "presence" side of the claim (SE beats self-consistency when clustering rules diverge) that v1 could only argue for by absence, and the design (SE clusters on parsed integer, SC on literal rendered string) cleanly isolates the mechanism
- The paper is unusually careful about calibrating its own claims: §2 explicitly proves why the noise-free SE≈SC near-tie is close to definitional rather than a finding, and the discussion in §4 correctly scopes what each experiment does and doesn't establish
- Multi-seed replication (3 independent training runs) closes the round-1 concern about training-run variance being unaccounted for by the test-resampling bootstrap CIs alone
weaknesses:
- The paraphrase-noise experiment (unlike the main sweep) uses only a single trained model/seed, so it's unverified whether the noise-level-dependent SE-over-SC gap is itself robust to training-run variance the way the noise-free near-tie was shown to be
- The absolute effect size of the demonstrated SE-over-self-consistency advantage is small even at the highest noise setting (+0.022 AUROC at noise_p=0.9, +0.013 at noise_p=0.6), so while statistically significant, the practical magnitude of the "predicted advantage" this paper set out to demonstrate is modest within this synthetic domain
- The digit-length ablation remains the weakest part of the paper (1-digit: only 5 error labels; 3-digit: AUROC undefined at 100% error) and was not improved in this revision despite being flagged in the round-1 review
- Still no test with a real pretrained LLM or genuine linguistic paraphrase/NLI clustering (explicitly attributed to no internet access); the bridging claim that this explains SE's real-world advantage over self-consistency remains an analogy from a numeric-surface-form proxy, not a demonstration in the domain the claim is actually about
questions:
1. Did you check whether the paraphrase-noise gap (SE minus SC-surface) replicates across the same 3 seeds used for the noise-free multi-seed check, or only on the single model used in §3's paraphrase table?
2. Given the modest absolute AUROC gap even at noise_p=0.9 (0.022), do you have a sense of what noise level or renderer richness would be needed to produce a gap comparable in magnitude to what's reported in real NLG SE-vs-self-consistency comparisons?
3. For the digit-length ablation, would drawing multiple resampled problem sets per digit-length bucket (rather than one draw per condition) be feasible within the same CPU budget, to get a usable CI for the 2-digit condition and partially address the label-imbalance issue in 1- and 3-digit conditions?
